answer: **Resource isolation.** Correct data permissions decide which rows or objects a tenant may read or write; they do not partition the pool's finite connection slots, wait queue, quota budget or failure domain. A tenant whose requests are slow, unbounded or retrying can hold or exhaust shared connections, making other tenants wait or time out. Authorization answers which objects a request may touch, not how much shared capacity it may consume, so a correct tenant predicate cannot prevent noisy-neighbour interference or starvation in a common pool. Sharing a pool therefore needs explicit fairness, per-tenant admission or quotas, bounded waits, escape hatches, and a test that saturates shared downstream resources to measure the noisy-neighbour effect separately from confidentiality. Isolation is multidimensional - identity/authorization, data, resource and lifecycle/operations (or process, network, compute, data, cache, cryptographic and control plane) - and correctness in one dimension does not establish any other. A dedicated pool is justified only when measured noisy-neighbour cost exceeds its operational cost; a shared pool that strands capacity or fails to enforce quotas is a reversal condition rather than a deployment detail. Boundary: a correct database policy does not protect a shared cache, search index or background consumer, and transaction pooling cannot preserve session state across transactions. Confidence is high on the concern, medium on the exact control set.
